title: Birth in Talwandi
intro: Guru Nanak Sahib was born in Rai Bhoi di Talwandi (present-day Nankana Sahib, Pakistan) in 1469. His parents were Mehta Kalu Ji and Mata Tripta Ji; his elder sister was Bebe Nanaki Ji.
record: The village was within the Lodi Sultanate. Bahlul Lodi ruled Delhi from 1451. The SGPC and historical biographies differ over the exact traditional birthday observance.
tradition: The Janamsakhis describe his childhood spiritual curiosity; these narratives were compiled later and cannot be read as contemporary transcripts.
recap: Talwandi → 1469 → Mehta Kalu → Mata Tripta → Bebe Nanaki.
questions: Where was Guru Nanak born?
Who was his elder sister?
Which dynasty governed Delhi in 1469?

title: Education, Janeu & Sacha Sauda
intro: Traditional accounts describe Guru Nanak Sahib's education and his questions about religious knowledge. The Janeu sakhi associates a childhood initiation with a composition preserved on Ang 471.
record: Gurbani, Ang 471: ਦਇਆ ਕਪਾਹ ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਸੂਤੁ ਜਤੁ ਗੰਢੀ ਸਤੁ ਵਟੁ ॥ — compassion, contentment, self-restraint and truth are named as the components of a spiritual thread.
tradition: The Sacha Sauda sakhi remembers Guru Nanak Sahib sharing resources with people in need near Chuharkana. The conversation and precise amount of money belong to later narrative tradition.
recap: Janeu → Daya → Santokh → Jat → Sat; Sacha Sauda → Chuharkana.
questions: What four virtues form the spiritual Janeu?
Where is Sacha Sauda remembered?
What type of source preserves the detailed childhood narratives?

title: Sultanpur Lodhi & the Bein
intro: Bhai Jai Ram Ji, husband of Bebe Nanaki Ji, is traditionally credited with arranging Guru Nanak Sahib's employment at Daulat Khan Lodi's modikhana, or government storehouse, in Sultanpur Lodhi.
record: Guru Nanak Sahib married Mata Sulakhni Ji; their sons were Baba Sri Chand Ji and Baba Lakhmi Das Ji. Bhai Mardana Ji, associated with the rabab, was his musical companion.
tradition: Janamsakhi accounts describe a three-day disappearance in the Bein River followed by the declaration 'Na Ko Hindu, Na Musalman'. Traditional chronologies differ, commonly suggesting around 1499 or 1507.
questions: Who arranged the modikhana employment?
What instrument did Bhai Mardana play?
What is the status of the three-day river account?

title: First Udasi: Saidpur & Haridwar
intro: The traditional First Udasi traces Guru Nanak Sahib's journeys across northern and eastern India. The Puratan Janamsakhi divides the travels into four major Udasis; other collections differ.
record: At Saidpur (Eminabad), the Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago sakhi contrasts honest livelihood with exploitative wealth through a milk-and-blood narrative. The miracle is a traditional account.
tradition: At Haridwar, the Janamsakhi describes Guru Nanak Sahib throwing water westward, questioning the practice of offerings toward ancestors. Gurbani on Ang 1245 states: ਘਾਲਿ ਖਾਇ ਕਿਛੁ ਹਥਹੁ ਦੇਇ ॥ — earn through work and share.
questions: Who was Bhai Lalo?
What happens in the Haridwar water sakhi?
On which Ang is the verse about working and sharing?

title: Eastern Journey: Kashi to Kamrup
intro: Eastern journey traditions associate Guru Nanak Sahib with Banaras (Kashi), Gaya, Bengal and Kamrup (Assam). Their exact routes and dates cannot be independently reconstructed.
record: At Gaya, the Janamsakhi describes a discussion of ancestral rites. Guru Nanak Sahib's composition on Ang 358 begins: ਦੀਵਾ ਮੇਰਾ ਏਕੁ ਨਾਮੁ ਦੁਖੁ ਵਿਚਿ ਪਾਇਆ ਤੇਲੁ ॥ — the Divine Name is likened to a lamp.
tradition: The Nur Shah tale, including miraculous transformations of Bhai Mardana, is a Janamsakhi narrative rather than independently verified history. Dhubri preserves a later local tradition of a visit.
recap: Kashi → Gaya → Bengal → Kamrup; Ang 358 → lamp of Naam.
questions: Which city is known for ancestral rites?
What is the lamp in the Ang 358 composition?
Who is Nur Shah in the tradition?

title: Jagannath Puri & Gagan Mai Thaal
intro: Sikh tradition places Guru Nanak Sahib at Jagannath Puri in Odisha, an important pilgrimage centre, during his eastern or southern travels. The date and route differ among Janamsakhi traditions.
record: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 13, preserves: ਗਗਨ ਮੈ ਥਾਲੁ ਰਵਿ ਚੰਦੁ ਦੀਪਕ ਬਨੇ ਤਾਰਿਕਾ ਮੰਡਲ ਜਨਕ ਮੋਤੀ ॥ — the sky is the Aarti tray, sun and moon its lamps, and stars its pearls.
tradition: The association of the composition with a temple Aarti ceremony is a traditional biographical account. The Gurbani is preserved primary text, but does not itself specify Puri as the setting.
recap: Puri → Aarti → Gagan Mai Thaal → Ang 13.
questions: Which city is linked with Gagan Mai Thaal?
Which Ang preserves the composition?
What is the difference between the shabad and the Puri sakhi?

title: Southern Journey: Sri Lanka and Raja Shivnabh
intro:
The southern Udasi traditions describe Guru Nanak Sahib travelling from Odisha through the Deccan and peninsular India, with some accounts extending to Singhaldvip, conventionally identified as Sri Lanka. The Puratan and Miharban Janamsakhi collections do not organise all journeys identically. The described routes and precise years remain uncertain.

The early-sixteenth-century Deccan was politically diverse, with successor states of the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire. The traditions place Guru Nanak's discussions in this varied religious environment.
record: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji preserves Dakhni Oankar in Raag Ramkali, Angs 929–938. Its scriptural preservation establishes Guru Nanak's teaching, not a specific site or date of composition. J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, and Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I, provide historical context for the first Guru and his travels.
tradition: The Raja Shivnabh sakhi concerns a merchant called Bhai Mansukh, whose devotional conduct reportedly inspired a ruler of Singhaldvip to seek Guru Nanak's teaching. Accounts describe the Guru's arrival and the Raja's discipleship. The story belongs to the Janamsakhi tradition; its personal conversations and historical identification of the king are not independently established.
recap: Puri → southern route traditions → Singhaldvip → Raja Shivnabh. Bhai Mansukh is the merchant in the traditional account. Dakhni Oankar is preserved on Angs 929–938. Route and miraculous details should not be treated as verified.
questions: What is Singhaldvip traditionally identified with?
Who is the merchant in the Raja Shivnabh sakhi?
Which Angs preserve Dakhni Oankar?
references: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 929–938 (Dakhni Oankar)
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Raja Shivnabh
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab

title: Bidar and the Nanak Jhira Tradition
intro:
Bidar, on the Deccan Plateau, was a major centre of the Bahmani Sultanate, which transferred its capital there in the fifteenth century. Its fortifications, architecture and scholarship provide the historical setting for the Nanak Jhira tradition.

The site today commemorates Guru Nanak Sahib's purported visit and a spring near Bidar. The history of the physical shrine is distinct from the much earlier episode narrated in Sikh tradition.
record: Japji Sahib, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 8, includes ਪਵਣੁ ਗੁਰੂ ਪਾਣੀ ਪਿਤਾ ਮਾਤਾ ਧਰਤਿ ਮਹਤੁ ॥, depicting air, water and earth through familial imagery. That passage is authenticated scripture, but is not independently dated to Bidar. The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism's Bidar entry describes the shrine's later institutional history, including twentieth-century custodianship and construction.
tradition: The Nanak Jhira sakhi says that Guru Nanak Sahib and Bhai Mardana met religious faqirs near Bidar. Residents faced a drinking-water problem; the account describes a spring emerging when Guru Nanak moved a stone. Some versions name Pir Jalaluddin. The miraculous origin and exact conversations are traditional narratives, not independently established historical events.
recap: Bidar → Deccan → Nanak Jhira → freshwater spring. The spring and shrine exist; the reported miracle is tradition. Ang 8 names air, water and earth. Historical buildings and remembered events require different forms of evidence.
questions: Which Sultanate made Bidar a capital?
What is Nanak Jhira associated with?
On which Ang is 'Pavan Guru Pani Pita' found?
references: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 8 (Japji Sahib)
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Bidar
Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I

title: The Siddhas, Nath Yogis and Siddh Gosht
intro:
Nath yogic traditions were influential across North India. Their practices and centres formed an important context for Guru Nanak Sahib's engagement with renunciation, spiritual discipline and the householder's life.

Sikh travel traditions associate discussions with yogis at sites including Achal Batala and Tilla Jogian. A separate sacred-mountain setting, Sumer Parbat, occurs in traditional narratives; no exact itinerary can be reconstructed from these accounts.
record: Siddh Gosht appears in Raag Ramkali, Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 938–946. It records a dialogue addressing the Divine, Shabad, Naam, spiritual understanding and ascetic practices. The lotus and waterbird imagery on Ang 938 describes living amidst the world without attachment. Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 40, is an early Sikh literary source for the Achal encounter; it is not an eyewitness transcript.
tradition: Janamsakhi traditions describe Guru Nanak Sahib debating Nath yogis, including an encounter with Bhangar Nath at Achal Batala. Some retellings feature miraculous demonstrations. The narrative settings and dialogues vary across sources. The composition Siddh Gosht is primary scriptural evidence; a specific mountain meeting is not thereby independently proved.
recap: Nath yogis → Siddhas → dialogue with Guru Nanak. Siddh Gosht: Angs 938–946. Lotus and waterbird: live in the world while remaining unattached. Achal Batala is a traditional encounter site; its precise conversation is not independently verified.
questions: Where is Siddh Gosht preserved?
Which two natural images describe detachment?
Which yogi is linked with Achal Batala in Sikh tradition?
references: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 938–946 (Siddh Gosht)
Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 40
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Siddh Gosti; Achal Sahib

title: Mecca and Baghdad: Western Journey Traditions
period: Early sixteenth century; exact dates disputed
intro:
Sikh tradition describes Guru Nanak Sahib's western travels to Mecca, Medina and Baghdad. Early-sixteenth-century western Asia contained Ottoman, Safavid and Mamluk political spheres, as well as established Islamic scholarship and Sufi communities.

Although the stories are important within Sikh literature, exact dates, routes and individual encounters are not independently settled.
record: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauris 32–37, is an important early Sikh literary witness to the Mecca and Baghdad narratives, written after Guru Nanak's lifetime. Guru Nanak's Gurbani supplies direct testimony to his teachings about Divine presence; the location of a story must be established separately. V. L. Ménage's 1979 article in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society examines the disputed Baghdad inscription.
tradition: In the Mecca sakhi, someone objects to the direction of Guru Nanak's feet, and the narrative describes the sacred direction appearing to move as his feet are turned. The Baghdad account places Bhai Mardana beside Guru Nanak and describes discussions with a local religious figure. Miraculous details are traditional, and the Baghdad inscription's dating and identification remain disputed.
recap: Westward travels → Mecca → Baghdad. Bhai Gurdas preserves an early literary account, not an eyewitness journal. The Mecca sakhi concerns Divine omnipresence. The Baghdad inscription is contested, not conclusive evidence.
questions: Which Vaar of Bhai Gurdas recounts Mecca and Baghdad?
Who accompanies Guru Nanak in the Baghdad account?
What is the status of the Baghdad inscription?
references: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauris 32–37
V. L. Ménage, 'The Gurū Nānak Inscription at Baghdad,' Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (1979)
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab

title: Babur's Invasions and the Babarvani
intro:
Babur, the Timurid ruler based in Kabul, mounted campaigns into northwestern India. His defeat of Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat on 21 April 1526 inaugurated Mughal rule in northern India. Punjab's towns and residents experienced violence, captivity and disruption during these struggles.

Guru Nanak Sahib's compositions collectively called Babarvani are especially valuable because they address political events and suffering during his lifetime.
record: The four compositions collectively called Babarvani occur on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 360, 417–418 and 722–723. Ang 360 asks why such violence and crying out occurred. Ang 722 directly addresses Lalo and likens the invading army to a coercive wedding procession. These texts document Guru Nanak's response, rather than a detailed military chronicle.
tradition: Janamsakhi accounts associate Guru Nanak Sahib with Saidpur (Eminabad), captivity and a meeting with Babur; some versions describe a hand mill turning miraculously. Babur's campaigns are historically documented, but the precise conversations and supernatural events of the captivity story are not independently verified.
recap: 1519–1526 → Babur's campaigns; 21 April 1526 → Panipat. Babarvani: Angs 360, 417–418, 722–723. These compositions attend to civilians, women and political responsibility. The hand-mill sakhi is traditional.
questions: On which date was the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
Which Angs contain the Babarvani compositions?
Who is addressed in the Tilang composition on Ang 722?
references: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 360, 417–418, 722–723
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Babar Vani
Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I

title: Kartarpur: The First Sikh Community
intro:
Guru Nanak Sahib established a settled community at Kartarpur beside the Ravi in Punjab, commonly dated to around 1520–1522. Here his followers participated in agricultural work, congregation, devotional singing and communal meals.

Kartarpur became an enduring centre for the early Sikh community and the place where Guru Nanak spent his final years.
record: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 38, describes Guru Nanak returning to Kartarpur, setting aside travelling attire and living as a householder. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1245, states ਘਾਲਿ ਖਾਇ ਕਿਛੁ ਹਥਹੁ ਦੇਇ ॥ — earning through labour and giving from one's earnings. Early Sikh gathering places were commonly termed dharamsalas; later Gurus expanded the institutions of sangat and langar.
tradition: The Janamsakhi traditions describe land offered by a local official sometimes called Karori. The donor's identity and exact events differ in retellings, and no contemporary grant confirms every detail. Guru Nanak's later choice of Bhai Lehna as successor is a central tradition supported by additional early Sikh literature.
recap: Kartarpur → Ravi → farming → sangat → langar → dharamsala. Ang 1245: work and share. The Guru's settled life prepared the community for continuity after 1539.
questions: Beside which river was Kartarpur established?
Which Ang includes the verse about working and giving?
What was an early Sikh congregational place commonly called?
references: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 38
Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 1245
Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, Kartarpur
J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab

title: Bhai Lehna Becomes Guru Angad Dev Ji
intro:
Bhai Lehna, born in 1504 in Punjab, was associated in later Sikh biographies with devotional journeys to Jwalamukhi before he encountered Guru Nanak Sahib's teaching. He settled around Khadur and married Mata Khivi Ji.

Sikh tradition describes Lehna hearing Gurbani, travelling to Kartarpur, serving the congregation and ultimately being appointed Guru Angad Dev Ji. Guru Nanak chose him rather than either of his sons.
record: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 45, describes Guru Nanak appointing Lehna during his lifetime. The Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balwand on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 966, describes the succession using the continuity of spiritual light (jot) and way (jugat). These are stronger early literary and scriptural sources for the succession than the precise details of individual tests.
tradition: One traditional sakhi describes Bhai Lehna carrying muddy grass when others were unwilling, with some variants including a miraculous transformation of the mud. The account is preserved in later biographies, including M. A. Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion, Volume II. The service episode is traditional narrative, not a contemporary verbatim record.
recap: Lehna → Kartarpur → service → appointed Guru Angad in 1539 → Khadur Sahib. Bhai Gurdas Vaar 1 Pauri 45 and Ang 966 preserve early succession testimony. The muddy-grass tale is traditional.
questions: What was Guru Angad's earlier name?
Which Ang contains the Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balwand on the succession?
Did Bhai Gurdas say the appointment occurred during Guru Nanak's lifetime?
references: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ang 966, Ramkali ki Var of Satta and Balwand
Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 45

title: Guru Angad Dev Ji: Gurmukhi, Education, Akharas and Mata Khivi's Langar
intro:
After Guru Nanak Sahib appointed Bhai Lehna as Guru Angad, the young Sikh community faced a practical challenge: could it preserve its teachings and daily practices beyond its founder's lifetime? From 1539 to 1552, Guru Angad Dev Ji led the community from Khadur (Khadur Sahib), in present-day Tarn Taran district, Punjab. Kartarpur had been Guru Nanak's settled centre; Khadur became the next important gathering place. The community continued congregational worship, labour and shared food, while developing new forms of education and bodily training.

TIMELINE
1504 — Bhai Lehna, later Guru Angad, is born (traditional biographical chronology).
1539 — Guru Nanak appoints Lehna; Guru Angad succeeds him after Guru Nanak's death.
1539–1552 — Khadur is the principal centre of the second Guru. Sikh tradition associates this period with instruction in Gurmukhi, the strengthening of langar, and wrestling akharas.
1540 — Humayun loses his throne to Sher Shah Suri; a later sakhi places a meeting between Humayun and Guru Angad after this defeat, but its date and dialogue are unverified.
1552 — Guru Angad passes the Guruship to Amar Das and dies at Khadur (29 March is the widely received date).
1604 — The Adi Granth is compiled under Guru Arjan: a later stage of the scriptural preservation enabled by earlier literacy and manuscript practices.

PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Angad Dev Ji (1504–1552) — second Sikh Guru, formerly Bhai Lehna.
Mata Khivi Ji — Guru Angad's wife and a central figure in the Sikh communal kitchen.
Khadur Sahib — the second Guru's main centre.
Bhai Amar Das — disciple who would succeed as the third Guru.
Humayun and Sher Shah Suri — Mughal and Sur rulers whose conflict provides the historical setting for a traditional encounter.
Balwand and Satta — bards whose Ramkali ki Var preserves praise of Mata Khivi in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

The principal historical question is not whether Guru Angad 'invented' everything from nothing. It is how an existing Sikh fellowship became more durable through practices people could learn, repeat and pass to another generation.
record:
GURMUKHI AND LEARNING
Guru Angad is traditionally credited with refining, standardising and promoting Gurmukhi for the Sikh community. That does not mean he invented all its letters from nothing. Gurmukhi belongs to a wider family of northern Indian scripts and developed from earlier regional writing practices. Linguistic studies by Harjeet Singh Gill and Christopher Shackle, cited in Santbir Singh's Sikh Research Institute study (2026), describe this longer history. The historical contribution associated with Guru Angad is the script's more consistent form and its use for teaching and transmitting Gurbani.

Why did this matter? In sixteenth-century northern India, Persian served many court and administrative functions, while Sanskrit scholarship was associated with specialist learned communities. A script used for Punjabi-language teaching allowed learners to engage with the Guru's compositions more directly. Traditions describe children being taught at Khadur. The surviving evidence does not allow us to reconstruct a modern school timetable or to claim universal literacy, but the emphasis on reading and writing was significant for a developing community. Later Gurus expanded the copying and circulation of pothis (manuscript collections of Gurbani), leading ultimately to the compilation of the Adi Granth under Guru Arjan in 1604.

GURU ANGAD'S OWN GURBANI
The second Guru was not merely an administrator of Guru Nanak's legacy: saloks attributed to Mahalla 2 are preserved in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, often within the Vars. A well-known example in Asa di Var appears on Ang 463:
ਜੇ ਸਉ ਚੰਦਾ ਉਗਵਹਿ ਸੂਰਜ ਚੜਹਿ ਹਜਾਰ ॥
ਏਤੇ ਚਾਨਣ ਹੋਦਿਆਂ ਗੁਰ ਬਿਨੁ ਘੋਰ ਅੰਧਾਰ ॥੨॥
Close sense: even if a hundred moons and a thousand suns arose, without the Guru there would remain deep darkness. The image distinguishes physical illumination from spiritual understanding. Important textual precision: the hymn begins within Asa di Var, whose opening is on Ang 462, but THESE TWO LINES appear on Ang 463, under Mahalla 2. The exact Ang can be verified in the scripture and Professor Sahib Singh's Guru Granth Darpan.

MATA KHIVI AND LANGAR
Guru Nanak had already placed shared meals at the centre of community life. Under Guru Angad, Mata Khivi's leadership helped sustain and develop langar at Khadur. Its significance was not the invention of charitable feeding — other South Asian communities also fed pilgrims and travellers — but its recurring practice within a congregation where people of different backgrounds could sit and eat together.

We have unusually direct scriptural testimony for Mata Khivi. In the Ramkali ki Var attributed to Satta and Balwand, Ang 967, the text reads:
ਬਲਵੰਡ ਖੀਵੀ ਨੇਕ ਜਨ ਜਿਸੁ ਬਹੁਤੀ ਛਾਉ ਪਤ੍ਰਾਲੀ ॥
ਲੰਗਰਿ ਦਉਲਤਿ ਵੰਡੀਐ ਰਸੁ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤੁ ਖੀਰਿ ਘਿਆਲੀ ॥
The verse calls Khivi a noble person whose shade shelters others, and describes the bounty distributed in langar, including kheer enriched with ghee. It is praise preserved in the scripture, not a later invented quotation. Mata Khivi appears as a named participant in the early community's history, not only as the Guru's spouse. The verse should not be read as a full inventory of the kitchen or proof of every later langar custom.

AKHARAS AND PHYSICAL TRAINING
Historical Sikh accounts also associate Guru Angad with wrestling grounds, called mall akharas. Such spaces encouraged bodily discipline, strength and endurance. This does not mean that the later institutions of Sikh military organisation already existed in the 1540s. The later Gurus' political and military developments belong to their own periods. At Khadur, the historical tradition presents physical training alongside reading Gurbani, congregational worship and service. The evidence for the precise daily routine is mostly later biographical and institutional tradition, not a surviving attendance register.

PRESERVATION AND CONTINUITY
Khadur was a working religious centre rather than merely a memorial. Teaching Gurmukhi made scriptural transmission more accessible; langar required organised cooperation; the akhara offered communal physical discipline. Together these practices strengthened the community's ability to continue after the death of an individual Guru. J. S. Grewal's The Sikhs of the Punjab, chapter 'Evolution of the Sikh Panth (1539–1606)', and Khushwant Singh's A History of the Sikhs, Volume I, the chapters on early Sikh institutional development, place these developments in the longer growth of the Panth.
tradition:
SOURCE-BASED SAKHI: HUMAYUN'S VISIT TO KHADUR
After Babur's son Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah Suri, the Mughal ruler lost control of northern India in 1540. A later Sikh narrative says that, during his flight, Humayun visited Guru Angad at Khadur seeking spiritual assistance. The Guru was absorbed in worship or listening to kirtan and did not immediately attend to the ruler. The account says Humayun became angry and reached for his sword. Guru Angad rebuked him for threatening peaceful worshippers after failing to prevail against Sher Shah in battle. Humayun is then said to have regretted his behaviour.

The episode is presented in Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Volume II, 'Life of Guru Angad', Chapter IV. It also appears in later popular Sikh retellings. Different versions disagree about whether the sword was drawn or could not be drawn, and they supply differing dialogue. Macauliffe was recording earlier religious narratives centuries after the supposed event; his prose is not an eyewitness transcript. Humayun's defeat and exile are historically established, but the exact meeting at Khadur and the words spoken are not independently verified. The sakhi should therefore be read as a traditional account about humility and the limits of royal power, not as a securely documented audience with the emperor.

This distinction is important throughout the course: a historical ruler and a historical Guru may both be well attested, while a memorable story connecting them still requires separate evidence.
recap:
RECAP
1539–1552: Guru Angad Dev Ji leads the Sikh community from Khadur Sahib. He is associated with refining and teaching Gurmukhi, not inventing every letter from nothing. His own salok about a hundred moons and a thousand suns appears on Ang 463, Mahalla 2. Mata Khivi Ji's langar is directly praised by Satta and Balwand on Ang 967. Wrestling akharas are part of the historical tradition of physical training at Khadur. The Humayun encounter is a later sakhi, not an independently verified transcript. In 1552 Guru Angad's successor was Guru Amar Das Ji.

title: Guru Amar Das Ji: Goindwal, Seva, Pangat and the Manji Network
intro:
Guru Angad Dev Ji's successor was not a young relative or a powerful local official. Guru Amar Das Ji (traditionally 1479–1574) became the third Sikh Guru in 1552, when he was approximately 73. His period of leadership is associated with the growth of Goindwal, the organisation of regional sangats, the strengthening of langar and the composition of Anand Sahib. In the previous lesson, we examined Guru Angad's promotion of Gurmukhi, education, akharas and Mata Khivi Ji's langar at Khadur. Here we follow the next stage: how could a growing community serve people who lived far from the Guru's immediate presence?

DATED TIMELINE
1479 — Traditional birth year of Amar Das at Basarke near Amritsar. The exact birthday in modern calendars varies by source.
c. 1540 — According to later Sikh biographical accounts, Amar Das hears Guru Nanak's hymn sung by Bibi Amro, Guru Angad's daughter, and visits Khadur. The exact year is not independently established.
1540s–1552 — He serves Guru Angad's community; stories of water-carrying and early-morning service belong to later Sikh narrative sources.
1552 — Guru Angad appoints Amar Das as the third Guru. Goindwal becomes the central location of the Guruship.
1552–1574 — Traditions associate this period with the baoli at Goindwal, a network of 22 manjis, expanded pangat and langar, and major scriptural compositions.
1560s — Goindwal becomes an increasingly prominent religious centre. Some accounts date Emperor Akbar's visit to this decade, but the date and particulars are uncertain.
1574 — Guru Amar Das appoints Bhai Jetha (Guru Ram Das) as successor and dies at Goindwal.
1604 — Guru Arjan's Adi Granth includes Guru Amar Das's bani, including Anand Sahib, a later compilation event distinct from the original composition.

PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Amar Das Ji — third Guru, traditionally born in Basarke and active as Guru at Goindwal from 1552 to 1574.
Bibi Amro Ji — daughter of Guru Angad, central to the traditional account of Amar Das's encounter with Gurbani.
Guru Angad Dev Ji — second Guru who designated Amar Das as successor.
Goinda — local figure linked by tradition to the settlement at Goindwal.
Bhai Jetha — Guru Amar Das's son-in-law and successor, Guru Ram Das.
Emperor Akbar — Mughal emperor whose reputed meal in langar is a well-known later Sikh narrative.
Basarke — village near Amritsar; Khadur Sahib — Guru Angad's centre; Goindwal Sahib — town near the Beas that became Guru Amar Das's centre.

HISTORICAL FRAMEWORK
The middle decades of the sixteenth century saw Mughal power restored under Humayun in 1555 and consolidated under Akbar after 1556. The Sikh community grew within this changing political world. We should distinguish Guru Amar Das's own hymns, which are primary Sikh scriptural evidence, from later biographies that supply dates, conversations and miraculous details. J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, 'Evolution of the Sikh Panth (1539–1606)', and Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Volume I, discuss the early community's institutional development.
record:
GOINDWAL: FROM RIVER CROSSING TO SIKH CENTRE
Goindwal lies near the Beas River in present-day Tarn Taran district, Punjab. Tradition associates its early settlement with a person named Goinda and with the assistance of Amar Das during Guru Angad's lifetime. As Guru, Amar Das made Goindwal an important gathering centre for teaching, service and congregational life. The current gurdwara buildings and decorative features should not be mistaken for intact sixteenth-century structures. The town's history includes later rebuilding and commemoration.

The most famous physical feature is the baoli, a stepwell with 84 steps leading down toward water. Its practical function as a reliable water source and gathering place is historically intelligible in a busy settlement. The number 84 also carries religious associations with the traditional cycle of 8.4 million forms of life. Later devotional practices link the steps with recitation of Japji Sahib. It would be inaccurate to say that the existence of 84 steps proves every later claim about the ritual's origin or efficacy. Government of India's Incredible India heritage description identifies the baoli, its 84 steps and the association with Guru Amar Das.

PANGAT BEFORE SANGAT
Langar existed under Guru Nanak and was strengthened by Guru Angad and Mata Khivi. Guru Amar Das's period is remembered for making shared eating particularly prominent. The expression 'pahle pangat, phir sangat' means, approximately, first sit in the common row for food, then attend the congregation or meet the Guru. Pangat is the row of diners; sangat is the congregation. This matters in a society where caste and rank could affect who prepared food, who ate together and who sat apart. Eating the same meal in a common space was a recurring social practice, not simply a statement that everyone was equal. The exact phrasing of the slogan should not be presented as a verified verbatim sixteenth-century utterance.

The famous story that Mughal emperor Akbar sat in the langar before meeting Guru Amar Das is recorded in later Sikh tradition. It is plausible within the known reign of Akbar, but the precise visit, date, exchange and any related land-grant narrative are not independently established in the way the emperor's reign is. The point of the tradition is that even a ruler was expected to join the same meal as everyone else. Avoid treating this account as an eyewitness court record.

MANJI: LOCAL LEADERSHIP BEYOND GOINDWAL
As congregations spread beyond the Guru's immediate locality, Sikh historical tradition associates Guru Amar Das with the creation of 22 manjis. 'Manji' literally refers to a small cot or seat; here it denotes a regional seat of teaching and responsibility. Local leaders could teach Gurbani, organise congregations, facilitate service and maintain contact with the centre. This helped a network of sangats function across different places rather than depend on every follower travelling to Goindwal.

Accounts also mention women as teachers and a related network of pirhis. However, surviving lists and exact counts of subordinate seats vary among later sources. The familiar figure of 22 manjis is a widely received historical tradition, but it should not be confused with a surviving sixteenth-century administrative register. Similarly, the later masand system evolved over time; it is anachronistic to describe every manji leader as performing the identical role of a later masand. The institutional importance is the movement toward distributed religious leadership.

GURBANI: ANAND SAHIB, ANGS 917–922
Guru Amar Das's Anand Sahib appears in Raag Ramkali, Mahalla 3, beginning on Ang 917 and continuing through Ang 922 of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Its opening is:
ਅਨੰਦੁ ਭਇਆ ਮੇਰੀ ਮਾਏ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਮੈ ਪਾਇਆ ॥
A close rendering is: 'Joy has arisen, O my mother, for I have found the True Guru.' The next line connects the meeting with the True Guru to sahaj, spiritual poise. Anand Sahib is a forty-pauri composition in its complete form. It is recited in Sikh worship today; a shorter liturgical selection is also common. The scriptural text does not provide an exact date or location of its original composition. Its preservation in the Adi Granth compiled in 1604 is a separate, later event.

GURBANI AND SATI: ANG 787
In Raag Suhi, a salok attributed to Mahalla 3 on Ang 787 begins:
ਸਤੀਆ ਏਹਿ ਨ ਆਖੀਅਨਿ ਜੋ ਮੜਿਆ ਲਗਿ ਜਲੰਨੑਿ ॥
Close sense: 'Do not call those women sati who burn with their husbands' bodies.' The passage then redefines virtue through character and remembrance rather than death on a funeral pyre. It offers direct scriptural evidence for Guru Amar Das's rejection of treating widow-burning as spiritual achievement. Wider claims about formal social prohibitions, purdah reform, widow remarriage and the exact number of female preachers are reported in later histories and should be evaluated separately. The original Gurmukhi is accessible on Ang 787; Professor Sahib Singh's Guru Granth Darpan offers Punjabi commentary.

WHY THESE CHANGES MATTER
Goindwal provided a centre; the baoli provided water and a communal site; langar and pangat made shared participation visible; the manjis connected distant sangats; and Gurbani supplied a common body of teachings. None of these developments can be reduced to a single founding decree. Their significance is that they made the community more durable, with activities that could be repeated in different places. The next Guru, Guru Ram Das, would continue this process through the development of a new settlement that became Amritsar.
tradition:
SOURCE-BASED SAKHI: BIBI AMRO'S SINGING
According to Sikh biographical traditions, Amar Das had followed a Vaishnava devotional path and made pilgrimages before joining the Sikh community. He heard Bibi Amro Ji, a daughter of Guru Angad, singing a hymn associated with Guru Nanak. The words moved him to ask about their source. Learning that they came from Guru Nanak's teachings, he went to Khadur to meet Guru Angad. He then began years of service in the Guru's community, traditionally described as fetching water before dawn and assisting with communal work. The account appears in later Sikh biographies, including Max Arthur Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion, Volume II, Life of Guru Amar Das. Different versions provide different details of the hymn, timing and family relationships. We can responsibly describe this as an established Sikh religious narrative, not an independently verified recording of a particular morning in c. 1540.

This story gives Bibi Amro an active role in transmitting Gurbani. It also reminds us that the Sikh community did not grow solely through formal sermons from the Guru. Music, household relationships and everyday religious practice could bring new followers into contact with its teachings. The historical fact of Guru Amar Das's succession in 1552 is much firmer than the details of his first hearing of Bibi Amro's singing.

A second traditional episode concerns Akbar eating in pangat. Later Sikh narratives say the emperor accepted the common meal before meeting Guru Amar Das. His reign is independently documented, but the particular visit and dialogue are not confirmed by a contemporary court transcript. The account should be presented as a sakhi illustrating the communal practice, not as conclusive evidence of a specific imperial audience.

SOURCES AND EVIDENCE
Primary scripture is strongest for what Guru Amar Das taught: Anand Sahib on Angs 917–922 and the salok concerning sati on Ang 787. Historical reference works and Sikh traditions provide accounts of Goindwal, the 22 manjis and langar's expansion. The baoli and its steps can be observed today, but later commemorative buildings do not by themselves establish all events attributed to the sixteenth century.
recap:
RECAP
1479: traditional birth of Amar Das at Basarke. c. 1540: Bibi Amro's singing introduces him to Guru Angad in a traditional account. 1552: he becomes third Guru, with Goindwal as his centre. During 1552–1574, the community develops a major gathering place, the 84-step baoli, strong langar and pangat practices, and a regional network traditionally counted as 22 manjis. Anand Sahib is preserved on Angs 917–922; Guru Amar Das's critique of sati appears on Ang 787. 1574: Bhai Jetha succeeds him as Guru Ram Das.

NEXT: Guru Amar Das's succession to Guru Ram Das, the emergence of Ramdaspur and the foundations of Amritsar. The course continues chronologically through all ten Gurus and later Punjab history.

What did a manji represent, and how many manjis are traditionally associated with Guru Amar Das Ji?
On which Ang does Anand Sahib begin, and which Ang contains Guru Amar Das Ji's salok criticising the burning of widows?

title: Guru Ram Das Ji: Ramdaspur and the Foundations of Amritsar
intro:
LESSON 16 — MONDAY, 2 NOVEMBER 2026 — MORNING
Reading time: 9–10 minutes
Previously: Guru Amar Das Ji, Goindwal, pangat, the baoli and the manji network.

CENTRAL QUESTION
How did Bhai Jetha, later Guru Ram Das Ji, establish a new Sikh town that would eventually become Amritsar — and how do we distinguish the fourth Guru's work from what Guru Arjan and later generations built?

The previous lesson ended at Goindwal in 1574. Guru Amar Das had expanded the Sikh community through regional congregations, langar and a settled centre near the Beas. His successor was his son-in-law Bhai Jetha, remembered as Guru Ram Das (1534–1581). During only seven years as Guru, he oversaw the growth of a new settlement and the sacred pool around which the future city of Amritsar developed. The city was also a working economic community: craftspeople, traders, workers and visitors needed houses, markets, water and shared institutions. That practical aspect of its foundation matters just as much as its religious symbolism.

DATED TIMELINE
1534 — Bhai Jetha is born in Chuna Mandi, Lahore (the day/month differs between modern and traditional calendars).
c. 1540s — According to later biographies, orphaned Jetha lives with his grandmother at Basarke, sells cooked or roasted gram, and joins the developing Goindwal community.
1554 — Traditional date of his marriage to Bibi Bhani Ji, daughter of Guru Amar Das.
1574 — Guru Amar Das appoints Bhai Jetha as Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru.
c. 1570s, commonly 1577 — A new settlement and excavation of a major pool develop at Guru ka Chak / Ramdaspur. Exact foundation dates differ across historical accounts.
1581 — Guru Ram Das dies; his youngest son Arjan succeeds him.
1604 — Under Guru Arjan, the Adi Granth is installed in the Harmandir Sahib: this belongs to the fifth Guru's period, not the fourth.
1909 — The Anand Marriage Act recognises Sikh Anand marriages in law; the modern legal and ceremonial history must not be projected unaltered onto the 1570s.

KEY PEOPLE AND PLACES
Guru Ram Das Ji (Bhai Jetha) — fourth Guru, founder of Ramdaspur.
Guru Amar Das Ji — third Guru, his predecessor and father-in-law.
Bibi Bhani Ji — Guru Amar Das's daughter and Guru Ram Das's wife.
Prithi Chand, Mahadev and Arjan — the couple's three sons; Arjan became the fifth Guru.
Bhai Gurdas — early Sikh writer whose Vaar 1, Pauri 47, describes Guru Ram Das and the tank at Amritsar.
Baba Sundar — author of the Ramkali Sadd on Angs 923–924, a scriptural source for the succession.
Lahore — birthplace in present-day Pakistan.
Basarke and Goindwal — places connected to Jetha's upbringing and service.
Guru ka Chak / Ramdaspur / Amritsar — successive names associated with the new Sikh settlement.
Tung — village whose landholders appear in one version of the land-acquisition story.
record:
1. FROM LAHORE TO GOINDWAL
The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism identifies Jetha as born in 1534 in Lahore to Hari Das and Anup Devi (also called Daya Kaur). After losing his parents, he lived with his grandmother in Basarke. Stories about selling cooked beans or roasted chickpeas and giving food away are familiar in Sikh biographical tradition; precise conversations and individual acts cannot be established from contemporary records. At Goindwal he became known for serving the congregation and assisting Guru Amar Das. He married Bibi Bhani in 1554, according to the conventional chronology, and the family remained at Goindwal. Their sons were Prithi Chand, Mahadev and Arjan. The succession in 1574 was therefore within an extended family, but the early Sikh account still presents the Guru's designation as decisive rather than automatic inheritance.

2. AN EARLY SCRIPTURAL ACCOUNT OF THE SUCCESSION
The Ramkali Sadd by Baba Sundar, preserved in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 923–924, is a particularly valuable early Sikh literary source. On Ang 923 it describes Guru Amar Das assembling his family and community and publicly recognising Ram Das. The verse includes:
ਰਾਮਦਾਸ ਸੋਢੀ ਤਿਲਕੁ ਦੀਆ ਗੁਰ ਸਬਦੁ ਸਚੁ ਨੀਸਾਣੁ ਜੀਉ ॥
A close sense is that the ceremonial mark was bestowed on Ram Das Sodhi, with the Guru's Shabad as the true sign. This is scriptural testimony to the succession, although it is not a modern administrative record. Professor Sahib Singh's Sri Guru Granth Darpan, Ang 923, identifies the author Sundar and discusses the composition. The date of 1574 is conventional in Sikh history.

3. A TOWN WITH WATER, HOMES AND WORK
The site chosen for the new settlement lay roughly 40 km northwest of Goindwal, in the Majha region of Punjab. Tradition says Guru Amar Das had encouraged the search for a place where a town and pool could be established. The developing settlement was called Guru ka Chak and Ramdaspur; Amritsar became the later name associated with the sacred pool, amrit sar or 'pool of nectar'. Sources differ on whether the founding should be dated around 1570, 1574 or 1577. The exact sequence of excavation and completion is likewise disputed. It is safest to describe the foundation as a process during the 1570s rather than a single precisely verified ceremony.

There are also competing accounts of land acquisition. One, cited in the Encyclopaedia of Sikhism from the Amritsar District Gazetteer, says 500 bighas were purchased from landowners at Tung for 700 Akbari rupees. Another says Emperor Akbar granted land to Bibi Bhani after offering it to Guru Amar Das. Neither account should be stated as an undisputed sixteenth-century land deed. The competing versions reflect different traditions and later historical reporting.

The new centre required practical organisation. Excavating and maintaining a large water reservoir involved labour, provisions and continuing contributions. Houses were needed for workers and visiting families. Guru Ram Das invited merchants and artisans to settle, and the town grew into a commercial as well as religious centre. It is misleading to picture a completed Golden Temple already standing there in 1577. The Harmandir Sahib building and the 1604 installation of the Adi Granth belong to Guru Arjan's subsequent leadership.

4. BHAI GURDAS AS AN EARLY WITNESS TO THE TANK
Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 47, states:
ਬੈਠਾ ਸੋਢੀ ਪਾਤਿਸਾਹੁ ਰਾਮਦਾਸੁ ਸਤਿਗੁਰੂ ਕਹਾਵੈ।
ਪੂਰਨੁ ਤਾਲੁ ਖਟਾਇਆ ਅੰਮ੍ਰਿਤਸਰਿ ਵਿਚਿ ਜੋਤਿ ਜਗਾਵੈ।
In close sense: Ram Das was seated as the true Guru, and he had the pool dug, making Amritsar a centre of the Guru's light. Bhai Gurdas wrote after Guru Ram Das's lifetime, but much closer to these events than many later Janamsakhis or commemorative histories. The lines support the early Sikh community's association of the fourth Guru with the Amritsar pool. They do not resolve the exact year of the first excavation or prove the land-grant story.

5. LAAVAN: SCRIPTURE AND THE HISTORY OF THE MARRIAGE CEREMONY
Guru Ram Das composed the four Laavan (ਲਾਵਾਂ) in Raag Suhi, Mahalla 4, on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Angs 773–774. The first begins on Ang 773:
ਹਰਿ ਪਹਿਲੜੀ ਲਾਵ ਪਰਵਿਰਤੀ ਕਰਮ ਦ੍ਰਿੜਾਇਆ ਬਲਿ ਰਾਮ ਜੀਉ ॥
A close rendering is: in the first laav, the Guru establishes commitment to the way of remembering the Divine. The second stanza develops awareness of the Divine, the third describes longing and love, and the fourth speaks of sahaj and spiritual union. The text uses marriage imagery for the relationship between the soul and the Divine; its theological meaning is not limited to human marriage.

Today the four Laavan are sung during Anand Karaj, the Sikh marriage ceremony. But one must distinguish the sixteenth-century composition from the exact form of today's wedding ritual. Marriage customs varied among Sikhs in subsequent centuries; the modern form involving four circuits around Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji became more widely standardised in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The Anand Marriage Act was enacted on 22 October 1909. It would be inaccurate to assume that every modern ceremonial step was already fixed during Guru Ram Das's lifetime.

6. FROM MANJIS TO DISTANT SANGATS
The third Guru's period is associated with regional manjis. Guru Ram Das's growing centre needed contributions for the tank, langar and congregation. Sikh historical accounts associate his period with representatives gathering offerings and communicating with distant sangats, often described as an early stage in the masand system. However, reference works do not always agree on whether to credit the initial formal appointment of masands to Guru Ram Das or to Guru Arjan. It is safer to describe an evolving system than a complete bureaucracy founded in one year.

7. SUCCESSION IN 1581
Guru Ram Das's sons were Prithi Chand, Mahadev and Arjan. Sikh tradition describes disagreement surrounding the selection of the youngest son. The fourth Guru designated Arjan as successor in 1581. This introduced an important new stage: while the first three successions had not been straightforward father-to-son inheritance, Guru Arjan was the son of his predecessor. The role of designation, competing claims and the subsequent expansion of Amritsar will be examined in Lesson 17. Guru Arjan's later compilation of the Adi Granth in 1604 and the construction of the Harmandir Sahib should be studied as developments under the fifth Guru, not retroactively attributed to Guru Ram Das.

WHY IT MATTERS
Goindwal had shown how a congregation could be organised. Ramdaspur showed how the community could develop a permanent town with water infrastructure, trade, residential settlement and religious activity. Bhai Gurdas's early account and the Laavan supply firmer literary evidence than the details of later miracle stories. The foundation of Amritsar was an extended communal project, not a single building inaugurated fully formed.

SOURCES FOR THIS SECTION
Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, Ramkali Sadd by Baba Sundar, Angs 923–924; Suhi Mahalla 4, Laavan, Angs 773–774. Professor Sahib Singh, Sri Guru Granth Darpan, Angs 773–774 and 923–924. Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 47. Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Ram Das, Guru (1534–1581)' (Punjabi University). J. S. Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab, 'Evolution of the Sikh Panth (1539–1606)'. Khushwant Singh, A History of the Sikhs, Vol. I, early Gurus and institutional development. Basics of Sikhi, 'Guru Ram Das Ji – 4th Sikh Guru' (2022). India Code, Anand Marriage Act, 1909.
tradition:
SOURCE-BASED SAKHI: THE REBUILT PLATFORMS
A well-known traditional account describes Guru Amar Das asking two sons-in-law, Rama and Bhai Jetha, to construct raised platforms (tharas). When the platforms were completed, he rejected them and requested they be rebuilt. In the story Rama eventually refused to continue, while Jetha repeatedly rebuilt his platform without resentment. The Guru is said to have recognised Jetha's patience and humility and selected him as successor.

This account is presented in later Sikh biographies and summarised by the Sikh Missionary Society in The Teachings of Guru Amardas Ji, section 'Training and Succession of Bhai Jetha'. Versions differ in how many attempts are described and in the exact dialogue. The story is useful as a traditional account of the qualities associated with leadership, but the building test itself is not independently attested in a contemporary dated record. By contrast, Baba Sundar's Ramkali Sadd on Ang 923 directly records the recognition of Ram Das in the early Sikh scriptural tradition.

A second popular narrative says Jetha gave food away when he was poor; this likewise comes from later biography. It should not be treated as a verbatim childhood incident. The difference between these traditional stories and the better-attested appointment, pool construction and surviving Gurbani is a key historical distinction.
recap:
RECAP
1534: Bhai Jetha is born in Lahore. 1554: traditional marriage date with Bibi Bhani. 1574: he becomes Guru Ram Das. During the 1570s he oversees a new settlement, Guru ka Chak / Ramdaspur, and the excavation of the pool from which Amritsar later takes its name. Land-acquisition stories conflict: purchase from Tung villagers or an Akbar-associated grant. Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 47, connects the fourth Guru with the Amritsar tank. Baba Sundar's Ramkali Sadd, Ang 923, supports the succession. Guru Ram Das's four Laavan are on Angs 773–774, though today's Anand Karaj ceremony was standardised much later. In 1581, Arjan succeeds as fifth Guru. Next: Guru Arjan, the expansion of Amritsar and the making of the Adi Granth.
